# Wave Function Collapse examples *Every public declaration used below is listed, with its KDoc, in the codebase reference: [`wfc.kt`](reference/data.md#wfc-kt) and [`wfc_field.kt`](reference/data.md#wfc-field-kt). Start from [what's already in the box](reference/index.md).* Wave Function Collapse (WFC) is a constraint solver that is mostly used to make textures and maps. Give it a grid, a set of tiles, and a table of which tiles may sit next to which, and it fills the grid: every cell starts holding *every* tile as a possibility, and the solver repeatedly picks the cell with the fewest options left, commits it to one tile chosen by weight, and then propagates the consequences outward until nothing else can be narrowed. Repeat until every cell is decided. The name is an analogy with quantum mechanics; there is no physics involved. Usually the constraints are *learned*: you draw one small example of the thing you want, and the solver reads the adjacency table off it and produces more. Unlike noise or an L-system, you describe neither the output nor a process that makes it. You describe what is *locally legal*, and a search finds a whole arrangement that never breaks a local rule. That is why WFC output tends to look designed. It also fails the way constraint solvers fail: too many constraints and it deadlocks, too few and every cell is legal but the result is shapeless. Most of the work is in the rules, not the solver. ## Source files The solver is [`wfc.kt`](https://github.com/OpenEndedGroup/Field4/blob/main/src/jvmMain/kotlin/afield/simulation/automata/wfc.kt), with no dependencies beyond `java.awt.image` and `ImageIO`. The views that put it on the canvas (`ToHTML`, heatmaps, montages) are in [`wfc_field.kt`](https://github.com/OpenEndedGroup/Field4/blob/main/src/jvmMain/kotlin/afield/simulation/automata/wfc_field.kt). The solver covers: - **The core solver** on integer tile IDs — [`WfcSolver`](reference/data.md#wfc-kt-wfcsolver), with weighted Shannon-entropy cell selection, weighted collapse, and bitset propagation that reuses `LongArray` scratch rather than allocating per neighbour. - **Rules from a sample grid** (the *simple-tiled* model) and **rules from overlapping N×M patterns** (the *overlapping* model), learned from a PNG, a `BufferedImage` or a 2-D `FloatArray`. - **Rules by hand**, via `wfcRules { … }`. - **Configurable symmetric neighborhoods** — [`WfcNeighborhood`](reference/data.md#wfc-kt-wfcneighborhood) is not hardwired to von Neumann; `Moore`, `chebyshev(r)`, `manhattan(r)` and arbitrary offset sets all work, for learning *and* propagation. - **An explicit `step()`**, so the collapse is observable rather than a black box. That is what the animation further down is made of. Things it does not do, so you are not surprised: - **No backtracking.** A contradiction is terminal. The remedy is to start the attempt again, which is what `solveWithRetries` does (see [Contradictions, seeds and reproducibility](#contradictions-seeds-and-reproducibility)). - **Symmetry expansion for *patterns*, not for hand-authored tiles.** [`expandSymmetry`](reference/data.md#wfc-kt) closes a learned overlapping pattern set under the rotations and reflections of the square, which is what stops a model from believing in whichever orientation its source happened to contain most of ([Not pixels](#not-pixels-wfc-on-a-scalar-field) shows it). It does *not* exist for the simple-tiled model: most tileset formats let you declare a tile and ask for its four rotations, and here a rotated tile is still a different tile that you supply and constrain yourself, because rotating tile *art* is a question about your pixels rather than about adjacency. - **2-D only**, and the *output* never wraps. `wrapX` / `wrapY` on `fromSampleGrid` affect how the sample is *read*, not how the result is generated. - **No absolute position.** The rules are translation-invariant, so "sky belongs at the top" is not something WFC can know. You pin it yourself with `forceTile` (see [the overlapping model](#the-overlapping-model-and-absolute-position)). ## The model, by hand Before any image loading, the smallest thing that is recognisably WFC: three tile IDs and a table. The tiles form a chain (sea, sand, grass) and sand is the only thing allowed to touch both sea and grass. Nothing here is learned; every constraint is stated. Note that `allow` is **directional and symmetric**: `allow(WFC_EAST, a, b)` says "`b` may sit east of `a`", and therefore also "`a` may sit west of `b`". It does *not* say `a` may sit east of `b`. An undirected "these two may touch" is that call in both orders, which is a two-line helper rather than a built-in, because the directional form is the one you need the moment tiles stop being symmetric. ```diffstatic_runner {data-lang=kotlin screenshot="assets/wfc_examples/by-hand.png" wait="1.5" capture="box" open-outputs="true" w="1200" name="wfc-by-hand"} :::static val SEA = 0 val SAND = 1 val GRASS = 2 val names = ["sea", "sand", "grass"] // The primitive is directional. "May touch", for tiles that have no orientation, is that // primitive applied both ways round in both authored directions. fun WfcRulesBuilder.mayTouch(a: Int, b: Int) { for (d in [WFC_EAST, WFC_SOUTH]) { allow(d, a, b) allow(d, b, a) } } val rules = wfcRules(tileCount = 3) { weights(3.0, 1.0, 3.0) // sea and grass equally likely; sand rare, so it stays an interface mayTouch(SEA, SEA) mayTouch(SEA, SAND) mayTouch(SAND, SAND) mayTouch(SAND, GRASS) mayTouch(GRASS, GRASS) // Note what is absent: mayTouch(SEA, GRASS). That single omission is the whole model. } val solver = WfcSolver(width = 22, height = 14, rules = rules, seed = 12L) // Seed both phases: sea pinned down the left edge, grass down the right. Without this the field // simply phase-separates — with only a one-cell-wide legal interface between them, whichever of // the two nucleates first tends to fill the whole grid. (The scalar field below shows that happening.) val outcome = solver.solveWithRetries { for (row in 0 until 14) { forceTile(0, row, SEA) forceTile(21, row, GRASS) } } val grid = solver.resolvedTileGridOrNull()!! // Read the table back out of the model rather than restating it from the source above. val table = (0..2).joinToString("
") { a -> "may sit east of ${names[a]}: " + (0..2).filter { rules.allows(WFC_EAST, a, it) }.joinToString(", ") { names[it] } } :::fold render the rule table and the tallies // One display() per channel: a second display() on the same channel REPLACES the first. markdown("rules", """ $table solved in ${outcome.attempts} attempt(s) · symmetric: ${rules.findAsymmetry() ?: "yes"} ${grid.count { it == SEA }} sea, ${grid.count { it == SAND }} sand, ${grid.count { it == GRASS }} grass of ${grid.size} cells """) :::endfold :::fold render one flat colour per cell, big enough to count them val palette = [ Triple(0.07f, 0.20f, 0.33f), Triple(0.85f, 0.78f, 0.55f), Triple(0.28f, 0.52f, 0.22f) ] val img = Img.generateRGB(22, 14) { x, y -> palette[grid[x + y * 22]] } showImgGrid("22x14 cells, seed 12" to img.upscaleNearest(26), columns = 1, cellSide = 700) :::endfold ``` ![a sea region and a grass region separated by a one-cell sand coastline, with the adjacency table beside it](assets/wfc_examples/by-hand.png) Sand appears exactly where it has to: as a one-cell-wide coastline wherever sea meets grass, because that is the only arrangement the table permits. Nowhere does sea touch grass. The solver was not told to draw coastlines. It was told that a sea-grass edge is illegal, and coastlines are what is left. That is also the first thing to check on any WFC result: **every adjacent pair in the output must be a pair the rules allow.** `allows` is there so you can assert it. The solver itself depends on adjacency being *symmetric*, that is, `allows(d, a, b) == allows(opposite(d), b, a)`. Propagation only ever pushes constraints outward from a cell that changed, one direction per arc, so an asymmetric rule set has arcs the solver structurally cannot check and it will emit pairs its own rules forbid. `findAsymmetry()` is that check. ## Learning from an image: the simple-tiled model Now the usual way round. `sliceIntoUniqueTiles` cuts a source image into fixed-size tiles, dedupes them, and hands back both the tile atlas and the grid of IDs it came from; `toRules()` then reads the adjacency table straight off that grid: every pair of neighbours it saw becomes a legal pair, and how often each tile occurred becomes its weight. The tile size goes all the way down to `1 × 1`, and at that size the model is at its most legible: a tile is then just a colour, and "learning the rules" is literally "note which colours were seen touching". ```diffstatic_runner {data-lang=kotlin screenshot="assets/wfc_examples/simple-tiled.png" wait="1.5" capture="box" open-outputs="true" w="1200" name="wfc-simple-tiled"} :::static :::fold build the source: three gaussian bumps minus a lake, quantised into five terrain bands fun bump(u: Double, v: Double, cx: Double, cy: Double, r: Double): Double { val dx = u - cx val dy = v - cy return exp(-(dx * dx + dy * dy) / (2.0 * r * r)) } val palette = [ Triple(0.08f, 0.20f, 0.31f), // deep water Triple(0.18f, 0.48f, 0.66f), // shallow water Triple(0.85f, 0.78f, 0.55f), // sand Triple(0.31f, 0.55f, 0.24f), // grass Triple(0.12f, 0.29f, 0.14f) // forest ] val sw = 26 val sh = 18 // Keep the band index per cell as well as the picture: it is what lets the histogram below talk // about terrain instead of about opaque tile IDs. val bands = IntArray(sw * sh) for (cy in 0 until sh) for (cx in 0 until sw) { val u = cx / (sw - 1.0) val v = cy / (sh - 1.0) val e = bump(u, v, 0.30, 0.40, 0.25) + 0.90 * bump(u, v, 0.70, 0.62, 0.21) + 0.55 * bump(u, v, 0.82, 0.22, 0.13) - 0.62 * bump(u, v, 0.34, 0.44, 0.085) bands[cx + cy * sw] = if (e < 0.16) 0 else if (e < 0.32) 1 else if (e < 0.44) 2 else if (e < 0.74) 3 else 4 } val source = Img.generateRGB(sw, sh) { x, y -> palette[bands[x + y * sw]] } :::endfold // One pixel per tile. Five bands in, five unique tiles out. val tiles = source.toBufferedImage().sliceIntoUniqueTiles(1, 1) val rules = tiles.toRules() // Tile IDs are discovery order, not band order. sampleIds is row-major over the same grid the // source was drawn on, so one pass recovers the correspondence both ways. val bandOfTile = IntArray(tiles.tileCount) val tileOfBand = IntArray(palette.size) for (cy in 0 until sh) for (cx in 0 until sw) { val i = cx + cy * sw bandOfTile[tiles.sampleIds[i]] = bands[i] tileOfBand[bands[i]] = tiles.sampleIds[i] } val outW = 40 val outH = 26 fun solveWith(model: WfcRules): IntArray { val solver = WfcSolver(outW, outH, model, seed = 12L) solver.solveWithRetries(maxAttempts = 30) return solver.resolvedTileGridOrNull()!! } val learned = solveWith(rules) // The learned weights are just a DoubleArray, and the solver reads it live — so a learned model is // editable. Boost the rare bands, and above all the *interface* band, sand. val reweighted = tiles.toRules() reweighted.weights[tileOfBand[0]] *= 2.0 // deep water reweighted.weights[tileOfBand[1]] *= 1.5 // shallow water reweighted.weights[tileOfBand[2]] *= 10.0 // sand, the only band that may touch both sides val boosted = solveWith(reweighted) val bandNames = ["deep", "shallow", "sand", "grass", "forest"] fun histogram(cells: IntArray, bandOf: (Int) -> Int): String = palette.indices.joinToString(" ") { b -> bandNames[b] + " " + (cells.count { bandOf(it) == b } * 100 / cells.size).toString().padStart(2) + "%" } :::fold render the three band histograms as text val bandReport = "source ${histogram(bands) { it }}\n" + "learned ${histogram(learned) { bandOfTile[it] }}\n" + "boosted ${histogram(boosted) { bandOfTile[it] }}" markdown("bands", """ ~~~ $bandReport ~~~ """) :::endfold // Scale factors chosen so every panel is 360px tall: montage gives each cell the height of the // tallest one, so mismatched panels leave a big empty band. showImgGrid( "source 26x18" to source.upscaleNearest(20), "learned weights" to tiles.toImg(learned, outW, outH).upscaleNearest(14), "sand boosted x10" to tiles.toImg(boosted, outW, outH).upscaleNearest(14), columns = 1, cellSide = 620 ) ``` ![the island source above two WFC outputs: learned weights lose all water, sand boosted x10 restores lakes with deep cores ringed by shallow](assets/wfc_examples/simple-tiled.png) The middle panel is correct: every adjacent pair in it is a pair present in the source. It is also nothing like the source: a speckle of grass and forest with a little sand and, as the histogram shows, no water at all, where the source was about a quarter water. Every seed does this, because the model is *bistable*. Grass and forest are the source's majority bands and they may touch each other, so they form a mutually reinforcing phase; water is a minority band reachable only across a one-cell sand interface, and once the first few cells commit to land there is no path back. Whichever phase nucleates first fills the grid. The bottom panel is the same rules with three weights multiplied. `rules.weights` is a plain `DoubleArray` that the solver reads live, so a learned model is editable. Boosting *sand*, the only band allowed to touch both sides, is the move: interface cells are what let the two phases sit near each other, so making them cheap lets all five bands coexist. It does not, however, reproduce the source's proportions: sand is now far more common than it ever was in the source. This model cannot reproduce global proportions, because it does not represent them. It is a table of which colours may touch plus a marginal frequency per colour; "water covers about a quarter of the map in large connected regions" is not expressible in that language, so no amount of weight tuning will produce it. ### The same source, with context The diagnosis points somewhere specific. A cell that holds one colour can only ever learn which colours touch, and the source's structure (a coast is water, then a *one-cell* sand fringe, then land) is a statement about a run of three cells, which a one-cell alphabet cannot hold. So give each cell more to hold. That is the **overlapping model**, and it is the answer to the figure above; [The overlapping model](#the-overlapping-model-and-absolute-position) has the rest of it. Instead of cutting the source into disjoint tiles, slide an N×N window over every position and keep the distinct windows you find; each solver cell now stands for one whole window, and two cells may be neighbours only if their windows *agree where they overlap*. Nothing else changes: same solver, same four directions, same learned weights. Each cell simply knows nine pixels instead of one. ```diffstatic_runner {data-lang=kotlin screenshot="assets/wfc_examples/terrain-overlapping.png" wait="4.0" timeout="180" capture="box" open-outputs="true" w="1200" name="wfc-terrain-overlapping"} :::static :::fold the terrain source from above, unchanged — one pixel per cell fun bump(u: Double, v: Double, cx: Double, cy: Double, r: Double): Double { val dx = u - cx val dy = v - cy return exp(-(dx * dx + dy * dy) / (2.0 * r * r)) } val palette = [ Triple(0.08f, 0.20f, 0.31f), // deep water Triple(0.18f, 0.48f, 0.66f), // shallow water Triple(0.85f, 0.78f, 0.55f), // sand Triple(0.31f, 0.55f, 0.24f), // grass Triple(0.12f, 0.29f, 0.14f) // forest ] val sw = 26 val sh = 18 val bands = IntArray(sw * sh) for (cy in 0 until sh) for (cx in 0 until sw) { val u = cx / (sw - 1.0) val v = cy / (sh - 1.0) val e = bump(u, v, 0.30, 0.40, 0.25) + 0.90 * bump(u, v, 0.70, 0.62, 0.21) + 0.55 * bump(u, v, 0.82, 0.22, 0.13) - 0.62 * bump(u, v, 0.34, 0.44, 0.085) bands[cx + cy * sw] = if (e < 0.16) 0 else if (e < 0.32) 1 else if (e < 0.44) 2 else if (e < 0.74) 3 else 4 } val source = Img.generateRGB(sw, sh) { x, y -> palette[bands[x + y * sw]] } :::endfold // The one changed line: 3x3 windows of the source instead of its five colours. wrapY = false so // the model never learns that the top of the map sits above the bottom of it. val patterns = source.toBufferedImage().sliceIntoOverlappingPatterns(3, 3, wrapX = false, wrapY = false) val rules = patterns.toRules() val outW = 40 val outH = 26 // Twelve seeds, because one picture of a stochastic process is an anecdote. No pinning, no // re-weighting: this is the learned model exactly as `toRules()` handed it over. val seeds = [1L, 3L, 5L, 7L, 9L, 11L, 12L, 17L, 23L, 42L, 101L, 2026L] val panels = mutableListOf>() var firstAttempt = 0 for (seed in seeds) { val solver = WfcSolver(outW, outH, rules, seed = seed) val outcome = solver.solveWithRetries(maxAttempts = 30) if (outcome.attempts == 1) firstAttempt++ val grid = solver.resolvedTileGridOrNull() ?: continue panels.add("seed $seed" to patterns.toImg(grid, outW, outH).upscaleNearest(6)) } // Why this figure has no ground constraint, read out of the model rather than asserted. The source's // corner is deep water, so that pixel identifies the band without re-deriving the palette's rounding. // // An explicit loop with a typed `px`, not `.first { ... .all { it == deepArgb } }`: a box's scope is // crowded enough that `all` inside a nested lambda whose receiver has no written-down type resolves // to something else entirely, and the error surfaces on a later line. val deepArgb: Int = source.toBufferedImage().getRGB(0, 0) var uniformDeep: Int = -1 for (id in 0 until patterns.tileCount) { val px: IntArray = patterns.patterns[id] if (px.all { v -> v == deepArgb }) { uniformDeep = id break } } val successors: String = (0..3).joinToString(" ") { d -> "dir " + d + " " + rules.allowedCount(d, uniformDeep) } :::fold render the model summary val modelReport = "${patterns.tileCount} distinct 3x3 windows · ${panels.size}/${seeds.size} seeds solved, " + "$firstAttempt on the first attempt\n" + "the all-deep window may be followed by: " + successors markdown("model", """ ~~~ $modelReport ~~~ """) :::endfold display("main", montage(panels, columns = 4, cellSide = 300).toPngBytes()) ``` ![twelve WFC outputs from the same terrain source, each a coastline sweeping across the frame with a sand fringe and mottled forest and grass inland](assets/wfc_examples/terrain-overlapping.png) Every adjacent pair in every output is a pair the source contained. These are coastlines, not islands. The model reproduces the source's local rules: the bands appear in chain order, every land-water boundary carries a one-cell sand fringe, and forest sits inside grass and never touches water. It does not reproduce the way the source arranges all of this into one closed ring, because that is a fact about the whole picture and an adjacency table only knows about neighbours. Each output is best read as a crop of a much larger world, and a coast running across a crop is a correct answer. The outputs are, if anything, more coherent than the source: neighbouring cells hold the same band more often than they do in the source, since the model has learned that interiors are large and boundaries thin, and nothing asks it to put a shoreline anywhere in particular. No cell is pinned in this figure, and the readout in the box says why: ```diffstatic {data-lang=text} the all-deep window may be followed by: dir 0 4 dir 1 2 dir 2 1 dir 3 1 ``` South and west, the all-deep-water 3 × 3 window has **exactly one** legal successor: itself. For a window to sit south of it, that window's top two rows must be entirely deep, and this source's water band is mostly thinner than three cells, so no such window exists except the uniform one. Pin a single cell to it and propagation paints the entire grid deep; add a second pin anywhere on land and you get an instant contradiction, on every seed and every retry. Any uniform window drawn from a band thinner than the window behaves this way, and `allowedCount` is how you find one. The 2 × 2 model has no such window (its all-deep window has 2–4 successors per direction) but produces visibly shattered, one-cell-speckled coastlines, so 3 × 3 is the pick here. ### 3 × 3 windows, not 2 × 2 tiles Both give a cell more context, and `sliceIntoUniqueTiles(2, 2)` looks like the cheaper way to get it (fewer tiles than there are 3 × 3 patterns). It costs more than it saves, and not only on this source. Bigger disjoint tiles mean most tiles are seen exactly once, at a sample edge, which leaves their mask in some direction empty. `fromSampleGrid` then widens each empty mask to "any tile may sit there", and because adjacency has to stay symmetric, filling one mask must *also* tell every other tile that this one may sit on its far side. One empty mask therefore adds `2 × tileCount` pairs: "anything may sit east of `t`" is an enormous claim. On this source a handful of empty masks leave 71% of the table invented by the fallback rather than observed, and the outputs then contain band pairs the source never contained. At `1 × 1` nothing is empty and nothing is invented, so the speckled figure above stays trustworthy as *evidence about the model* where a `2 × 2` version of it would not. So: ask. `widenedMaskCount` says whether the fallback fired at all, `wasWidened(direction, tile)` says where, and `observedAllows` is `allows` restricted to what the sample actually showed: the predicate to assert a learned model against, since `allows` on a widened table permits a great deal it never saw. The inline rules view in [Looking at the rules](#looking-at-the-rules) paints invented pairs amber for the same reason. ## Tiles with structure: the circuit set Context is one way to give the model more to work with. The other is to put the structure in the tiles themselves. When each tile carries internal art whose *edges* have to line up, the tile set encodes structure that a flat colour cannot, and the same solver produces something that looks constructed rather than grown. Nothing here is learned. This is an eight-tile set of circuit traces with rules derived from edge sockets. `b` may sit east of `a` exactly when `a`'s east socket matches `b`'s west socket. That is the original "simple tiled model", and it is about ten lines once the sockets are written down. ```diffstatic_runner {data-lang=kotlin screenshot="assets/wfc_examples/circuit.png" wait="1.5" capture="box" open-outputs="true" w="1200" name="wfc-circuit"} :::static // Sockets per tile, in WFC_NORTH, WFC_EAST, WFC_SOUTH, WFC_WEST order. 1 = a trace leaves this edge. val sockets = [ intArrayOf(0, 0, 0, 0), // blank intArrayOf(0, 1, 0, 1), // horizontal intArrayOf(1, 0, 1, 0), // vertical intArrayOf(1, 1, 0, 0), // elbow N-E intArrayOf(0, 1, 1, 0), // elbow E-S intArrayOf(0, 0, 1, 1), // elbow S-W intArrayOf(1, 0, 0, 1), // elbow W-N intArrayOf(1, 1, 1, 1) // cross ] // Edge matching, stated once. Everything else about the picture follows from it. val rules = wfcRules(tileCount = sockets.size) { weights(6.0, 2.0, 2.0, 1.0, 1.0, 1.0, 1.0, 0.35) for (a in sockets.indices) for (b in sockets.indices) { if (sockets[a][WFC_EAST] == sockets[b][WFC_WEST]) allow(WFC_EAST, a, b) if (sockets[a][WFC_SOUTH] == sockets[b][WFC_NORTH]) allow(WFC_SOUTH, a, b) } } :::fold draw 11x11 tile art from the same socket table: a centre pad plus a trace to each live edge val side = 11 val c = side / 2 val bg = 0xFF10241C.toInt() val trace = 0xFF64E0A0.toInt() val pad = 0xFFB8FFDA.toInt() // A top-level fun, not one nested inside the Array(...) lambda below: a local fun declared inside // a lambda in a Field box trips a K2 codegen assertion ("has no callableId"). fun traceArt(s: IntArray): IntArray { val px = IntArray(side * side) { bg } if (s[WFC_NORTH] == 1) for (y in 0..c) { px[c + y * side] = trace; px[(c - 1) + y * side] = trace } if (s[WFC_SOUTH] == 1) for (y in c until side) { px[c + y * side] = trace; px[(c - 1) + y * side] = trace } if (s[WFC_WEST] == 1) for (x in 0..c) { px[x + c * side] = trace; px[x + (c - 1) * side] = trace } if (s[WFC_EAST] == 1) for (x in c until side) { px[x + c * side] = trace; px[x + (c - 1) * side] = trace } if (s.any { it == 1 }) for (y in (c - 1)..c) for (x in (c - 1)..c) px[x + y * side] = pad return px } // A PngTileSet can be assembled from hand-drawn art; sampleIds is just the atlas row here, // because nothing is being learned from it. val tiles = PngTileSet(side, side, Array(sockets.size) { traceArt(sockets[it]) }, IntArray(sockets.size) { it }, sockets.size, 1) :::endfold val solver = WfcSolver(34, 22, rules, seed = 20260728L) val outcome = solver.solveWithRetries() val grid = solver.resolvedTileGridOrNull()!! // Separate channels rather than one montage: the atlas strip and the output have wildly different // aspect ratios, and a uniform grid would give the strip a cell 5 times taller than it needs. display("tiles", tiles.sampleToImg().upscaleNearest(6).toPngBytes()) display("main", tiles.toImg(grid, 34, 22).upscaleNearest(2).toPngBytes()) :::fold render the cell tallies markdown("counts", "${outcome.attempts} attempt(s) · ${grid.count { it == 7 }} crossings · " + "${grid.count { it == 0 }} blank of ${grid.size} cells") :::endfold ``` ![the eight-tile socket atlas above a 34x22 WFC output in which every circuit trace connects with no dangling ends](assets/wfc_examples/circuit.png) Every trace connects. There are no dangling ends anywhere in the output, and there cannot be: a live socket on one tile is only ever adjacent to a live socket on the next, so "wires join up" is a consequence of edge matching rather than something the generator tries to achieve. The weights are doing the aesthetic work. Blank is weighted 6 and the four-way cross 0.35, so the result reads as sparse circuitry rather than a dense maze. ## The overlapping model and absolute position [The terrain example](#the-same-source-with-context) used the overlapping model to fix a texture problem. Here is the rest of the mechanism, and the limit that no amount of context removes. First the trade, which is combinatorial. A 3×3 window over a 26×18 source can yield hundreds of distinct patterns where the simple-tiled model had five tiles, and both the rule-learning cost (it compares every pattern against every other) and the per-step entropy scan grow with that count. Larger windows are not free and are not automatically better: they buy coherence and they cost variety, because a window big enough to contain a whole feature can only ever reproduce that feature verbatim. And then the limit. The [terrain's](#learning-from-an-image-the-simple-tiled-model) coastlines were a success at reproducing local grammar and made no attempt at global composition, because WFC's rules are **translation-invariant**: they say what may sit next to what, and cannot say where anything belongs. That is not a texture problem and context does not touch it. The only cure is to supply position yourself, from outside the model, with `forceTile`. This source is built to make that visible: sky over soil, with flowers rooted in the soil. It is a correct answer (every 3×3 window in it appears in the source and every neighbouring pair agrees on its overlap), and it has no ground at all: a sky full of flowers whose stems run off the bottom edge with nothing to grow out of. Nothing in an adjacency table can say where anything belongs, so "the soil goes at the bottom" is not a fact this model has access to. The bottom panel's flowers are not the source's flowers: different columns, different heights, more of them than the source had. Note that `reset()` clears the whole wave, forced cells included. Boundary conditions therefore have to be re-applied on every retry, and `solveWithRetries` takes a `prepare` block to do it in. ## Neighborhoods beyond von Neumann `WfcNeighborhood` is a set of relative offsets plus the guarantee that every offset has its opposite in the set. `VonNeumann` is four offsets; `Moore` is eight; `chebyshev(r)` and `manhattan(r)` generate the obvious families, and `WfcNeighborhood.of(WfcOffset(2, 0), WfcOffset(-2, 0))` is as legitimate as either. The neighborhood is used for *both* learning and propagation, so widening it means the model observes more relations in the source and then enforces more of them in the output. Whether that matters depends entirely on whether the source has structure along the new offsets. Sweeping east it observes every possible pair (`A-A`, `A-B`, `B-B`, `B-A`) because a two-wide stripe means the colour changes on half the steps and stays on the other half. So the adjacency table ends up completely permissive, and the output is exactly what a completely permissive table produces: correct, and noise. Moore additionally observes the `(1, -1)` offset, where the colour is *constant*, and that one extra relation is enough to reproduce the stripes exactly: the break count in the box drops to zero. So choose the neighborhood to match the source; bigger is not better. On the five-band [terrain](#learning-from-an-image-the-simple-tiled-model) the diagonals are almost implied by the cardinals, and moving to Moore barely changes the picture. A wider neighborhood costs `directionCount` bitset intersections per propagation step and buys you nothing unless the source has something to say along those offsets. ## Watching the collapse `step()` is public and does exactly one WFC iteration: choose the lowest-entropy undecided cell, collapse it, propagate to a fixed point, return the new status. That is the right amount of work for a figure on a page and far too much for the thing you actually do a hundred times an hour while live coding, which is: look at the object. So `WfcSolver` implements `ToHTML`. Evaluating a solver (as a box's last expression, or via `.h` anywhere) draws its state instead of a reflective property tree. No tile set is needed, because none of these panels claims to show the tileset's colours:
| panel | colour means | scale | | --- | --- | --- | | possibilities left | how many tiles are still possible in that cell | `viridis`, fixed `1` (decided) … `tileCount` (untouched) | | entropy | weighted Shannon entropy, in nats — the quantity the solver actually minimises | `magma`, fixed `0` … `rules.fullSetEntropy()` | | decided tiles | which tile a cell settled on, as a stable hue per id | dark grey where still undecided |
The two heatmaps' domains are fixed by *meaning* rather than per frame, so successive looks at a running solver are comparable; auto-ranging is what makes an animated collapse appear to stand still. Values with nowhere to sit on a scale are taken off it and marked rather than clamped: a cell with **zero** possibilities is magenta in the count panel, because clamping 0 onto a `1..n` ramp would paint the one failure you need to see at the *decided* end and read as success. Entropy has a second such case. `fromSampleGrid` gives weight 0 to a tile the sample never contained, and a cell whose only survivor is such a tile has genuinely undefined entropy; those are drawn cyan, counted in the caption, and excluded from the range. Each caption names its colour scale and both endpoints in units. The two ramps are not interchangeable, because a marker colour is only a marker if it is *outside* the ramp it sits on. Drawn in `magma`, whose middle is pink and a shade away from the contradiction magenta, a perfectly healthy collapse frontier reads as a field of contradictions. It works on integer tile IDs, and the image helpers are a convenience layered on top, so the same machinery runs on a row-major `FloatArray` via `sliceIntoUniqueTiles2D` and `sliceIntoOverlappingPatterns2D`, and produces numbers rather than colours. Nowhere does sea touch grass. The solver was not told to draw coastlines. It was told that a sea-grass edge is illegal, and coastlines are what is left. That is also the first thing to check on any WFC result: **every adjacent pair in the output must be a pair the rules allow.** `allows` is there so you can assert it. The solver itself depends on adjacency being *symmetric*, that is, `allows(d, a, b) == allows(opposite(d), b, a)`. Propagation only ever pushes constraints outward from a cell that changed, one direction per arc, so an asymmetric rule set has arcs the solver structurally cannot check and it will emit pairs its own rules forbid. `findAsymmetry()` is that check. ## Learning from an image: the simple-tiled model Now the usual way round. `sliceIntoUniqueTiles` cuts a source image into fixed-size tiles, dedupes them, and hands back both the tile atlas and the grid of IDs it came from; `toRules()` then reads the adjacency table straight off that grid: every pair of neighbours it saw becomes a legal pair, and how often each tile occurred becomes its weight. The tile size goes all the way down to `1 × 1`, and at that size the model is at its most legible: a tile is then just a colour, and "learning the rules" is literally "note which colours were seen touching". ```diffstatic_runner {data-lang=kotlin screenshot="assets/wfc_examples/simple-tiled.png" wait="1.5" capture="box" open-outputs="true" w="1200" name="wfc-simple-tiled"} :::static :::fold build the source: three gaussian bumps minus a lake, quantised into five terrain bands fun bump(u: Double, v: Double, cx: Double, cy: Double, r: Double): Double { val dx = u - cx val dy = v - cy return exp(-(dx * dx + dy * dy) / (2.0 * r * r)) } val palette = [ Triple(0.08f, 0.20f, 0.31f), // deep water Triple(0.18f, 0.48f, 0.66f), // shallow water Triple(0.85f, 0.78f, 0.55f), // sand Triple(0.31f, 0.55f, 0.24f), // grass Triple(0.12f, 0.29f, 0.14f) // forest ] val sw = 26 val sh = 18 // Keep the band index per cell as well as the picture: it is what lets the histogram below talk // about terrain instead of about opaque tile IDs. val bands = IntArray(sw * sh) for (cy in 0 until sh) for (cx in 0 until sw) { val u = cx / (sw - 1.0) val v = cy / (sh - 1.0) val e = bump(u, v, 0.30, 0.40, 0.25) + 0.90 * bump(u, v, 0.70, 0.62, 0.21) + 0.55 * bump(u, v, 0.82, 0.22, 0.13) - 0.62 * bump(u, v, 0.34, 0.44, 0.085) bands[cx + cy * sw] = if (e < 0.16) 0 else if (e < 0.32) 1 else if (e < 0.44) 2 else if (e < 0.74) 3 else 4 } val source = Img.generateRGB(sw, sh) { x, y -> palette[bands[x + y * sw]] } :::endfold // One pixel per tile. It is also nothing like the source: a speckle of grass and forest with a little sand and, as the histogram shows, no water at all, where the source was about a quarter water. Every seed does this, because the model is *bistable*. Grass and forest are the source's majority bands and they may touch each other, so they form a mutually reinforcing phase; water is a minority band reachable only across a one-cell sand interface, and once the first few cells commit to land there is no path back. Whichever phase nucleates first fills the grid. The bottom panel is the same rules with three weights multiplied. `rules.weights` is a plain `DoubleArray` that the solver reads live, so a learned model is editable. Boosting *sand*, the only band allowed to touch both sides, is the move: interface cells are what let the two phases sit near each other, so making them cheap lets all five bands coexist. It does not, however, reproduce the source's proportions: sand is now far more common than it ever was in the source. This model cannot reproduce global proportions, because it does not represent them. It is a table of which colours may touch plus a marginal frequency per colour; "water covers about a quarter of the map in large connected regions" is not expressible in that language, so no amount of weight tuning will produce it. ### The same source, with context The diagnosis points somewhere specific. A cell that holds one colour can only ever learn which colours touch, and the source's structure (a coast is water, then a *one-cell* sand fringe, then land) is a statement about a run of three cells, which a one-cell alphabet cannot hold. So give each cell more to hold. That is the **overlapping model**, and it is the answer to the figure above; [The overlapping model](#the-overlapping-model-and-absolute-position) has the rest of it. Instead of cutting the source into disjoint tiles, slide an N×N window over every position and keep the distinct windows you find; each solver cell now stands for one whole window, and two cells may be neighbours only if their windows *agree where they overlap*. Nothing else changes: same solver, same four directions, same learned weights. Each cell simply knows nine pixels instead of one. ```diffstatic_runner {data-lang=kotlin screenshot="assets/wfc_examples/terrain-overlapping.png" wait="4.0" timeout="180" capture="box" open-outputs="true" w="1200" name="wfc-terrain-overlapping"} :::static :::fold the terrain source from above, unchanged — one pixel per cell fun bump(u: Double, v: Double, cx: Double, cy: Double, r: Double): Double { val dx = u - cx val dy = v - cy return exp(-(dx * dx + dy * dy) / (2.0 * r * r)) } val palette = [ Triple(0.08f, 0.20f, 0.31f), // deep water Triple(0.18f, 0.48f, 0.66f), // shallow water Triple(0.85f, 0.78f, 0.55f), // sand Triple(0.31f, 0.55f, 0.24f), // grass Triple(0.12f, 0.29f, 0.14f) // forest ] val sw = 26 val sh = 18 val bands = IntArray(sw * sh) for (cy in 0 until sh) for (cx in 0 until sw) { val u = cx / (sw - 1.0) val v = cy / (sh - 1.0) val e = bump(u, v, 0.30, 0.40, 0.25) + 0.90 * bump(u, v, 0.70, 0.62, 0.21) + 0.55 * bump(u, v, 0.82, 0.22, 0.13) - 0.62 * bump(u, v, 0.34, 0.44, 0.085) bands[cx + cy * sw] = if (e < 0.16) 0 else if (e < 0.32) 1 else if (e < 0.44) 2 else if (e < 0.74) 3 else 4 } val source = Img.generateRGB(sw, sh) { x, y -> palette[bands[x + y * sw]] } :::endfold // The one changed line: 3x3 windows of the source instead of its five colours. wrapY = false so // the model never learns that the top of the map sits above the bottom of it. val patterns = source.toBufferedImage().sliceIntoOverlappingPatterns(3, 3, wrapX = false, wrapY = false) val rules = patterns.toRules() val outW = 40 val outH = 26 // Twelve seeds, because one picture of a stochastic process is an anecdote. These are coastlines, not islands. The model reproduces the source's local rules: the bands appear in chain order, every land-water boundary carries a one-cell sand fringe, and forest sits inside grass and never touches water. It does not reproduce the way the source arranges all of this into one closed ring, because that is a fact about the whole picture and an adjacency table only knows about neighbours. Each output is best read as a crop of a much larger world, and a coast running across a crop is a correct answer. The outputs are, if anything, more coherent than the source: neighbouring cells hold the same band more often than they do in the source, since the model has learned that interiors are large and boundaries thin, and nothing asks it to put a shoreline anywhere in particular. No cell is pinned in this figure, and the readout in the box says why: ```diffstatic {data-lang=text} the all-deep window may be followed by: dir 0 4 dir 1 2 dir 2 1 dir 3 1 ``` South and west, the all-deep-water 3 × 3 window has **exactly one** legal successor: itself. For a window to sit south of it, that window's top two rows must be entirely deep, and this source's water band is mostly thinner than three cells, so no such window exists except the uniform one. Pin a single cell to it and propagation paints the entire grid deep; add a second pin anywhere on land and you get an instant contradiction, on every seed and every retry. Any uniform window drawn from a band thinner than the window behaves this way, and `allowedCount` is how you find one. The 2 × 2 model has no such window (its all-deep window has 2–4 successors per direction) but produces visibly shattered, one-cell-speckled coastlines, so 3 × 3 is the pick here. ### 3 × 3 windows, not 2 × 2 tiles Both give a cell more context, and `sliceIntoUniqueTiles(2, 2)` looks like the cheaper way to get it (fewer tiles than there are 3 × 3 patterns). It costs more than it saves, and not only on this source. Bigger disjoint tiles mean most tiles are seen exactly once, at a sample edge, which leaves their mask in some direction empty. `fromSampleGrid` then widens each empty mask to "any tile may sit there", and because adjacency has to stay symmetric, filling one mask must *also* tell every other tile that this one may sit on its far side. One empty mask therefore adds `2 × tileCount` pairs: "anything may sit east of `t`" is an enormous claim. On this source a handful of empty masks leave 71% of the table invented by the fallback rather than observed, and the outputs then contain band pairs the source never contained. At `1 × 1` nothing is empty and nothing is invented, so the speckled figure above stays trustworthy as *evidence about the model* where a `2 × 2` version of it would not. So: ask. `widenedMaskCount` says whether the fallback fired at all, `wasWidened(direction, tile)` says where, and `observedAllows` is `allows` restricted to what the sample actually showed: the predicate to assert a learned model against, since `allows` on a widened table permits a great deal it never saw. The inline rules view in [Looking at the rules](#looking-at-the-rules) paints invented pairs amber for the same reason. ## Tiles with structure: the circuit set Context is one way to give the model more to work with. The other is to put the structure in the tiles themselves. When each tile carries internal art whose *edges* have to line up, the tile set encodes structure that a flat colour cannot, and the same solver produces something that looks constructed rather than grown. Nothing here is learned. This is an eight-tile set of circuit traces with rules derived from edge sockets. `b` may sit east of `a` exactly when `a`'s east socket matches `b`'s west socket. That is the original "simple tiled model", and it is about ten lines once the sockets are written down. ```diffstatic_runner {data-lang=kotlin screenshot="assets/wfc_examples/circuit.png" wait="1.5" capture="box" open-outputs="true" w="1200" name="wfc-circuit"} :::static // Sockets per tile, in WFC_NORTH, WFC_EAST, WFC_SOUTH, WFC_WEST order. 1 = a trace leaves this edge. val sockets = [ intArrayOf(0, 0, 0, 0), // blank intArrayOf(0, 1, 0, 1), // horizontal intArrayOf(1, 0, 1, 0), // vertical intArrayOf(1, 1, 0, 0), // elbow N-E intArrayOf(0, 1, 1, 0), // elbow E-S intArrayOf(0, 0, 1, 1), // elbow S-W intArrayOf(1, 0, 0, 1), // elbow W-N intArrayOf(1, 1, 1, 1) // cross ] // Edge matching, stated once. There are no dangling ends anywhere in the output, and there cannot be: a live socket on one tile is only ever adjacent to a live socket on the next, so "wires join up" is a consequence of edge matching rather than something the generator tries to achieve. The weights are doing the aesthetic work. Blank is weighted 6 and the four-way cross 0.35, so the result reads as sparse circuitry rather than a dense maze. ## The overlapping model and absolute position [The terrain example](#the-same-source-with-context) used the overlapping model to fix a texture problem. Here is the rest of the mechanism, and the limit that no amount of context removes. First the trade, which is combinatorial. A 3×3 window over a 26×18 source can yield hundreds of distinct patterns where the simple-tiled model had five tiles, and both the rule-learning cost (it compares every pattern against every other) and the per-step entropy scan grow with that count. Larger windows are not free and are not automatically better: they buy coherence and they cost variety, because a window big enough to contain a whole feature can only ever reproduce that feature verbatim. And then the limit. The [terrain's](#learning-from-an-image-the-simple-tiled-model) coastlines were a success at reproducing local grammar and made no attempt at global composition, because WFC's rules are **translation-invariant**: they say what may sit next to what, and cannot say where anything belongs. That is not a texture problem and context does not touch it. The only cure is to supply position yourself, from outside the model, with `forceTile`. This source is built to make that visible: sky over soil, with flowers rooted in the soil. Every 3×3 window of it *says* something ("stem continues upward", "blossom sits on a stem", "stem meets soil") so the model has plenty to preserve, and it will still cheerfully put the soil nowhere at all. ```diffstatic_runner {data-lang=kotlin screenshot="assets/wfc_examples/overlapping.png" wait="2.0" capture="box" open-outputs="true" w="1200" name="wfc-overlapping"} :::static val SKY = Triple(0.75f, 0.86f, 0.94f) val SOIL = Triple(0.42f, 0.29f, 0.16f) val STEM = Triple(0.24f, 0.56f, 0.23f) val BLOSSOM = Triple(0.88f, 0.34f, 0.42f) val sw = 26 val sh = 18 val soilTop = 13 val flowers = [3 to 4, 8 to 6, 13 to 3, 18 to 5, 22 to 4] // column to stem height val source = Img.generateRGB(sw, sh) { x, y -> val flower = flowers.firstOrNull { it.first == x } when { y >= soilTop -> SOIL flower != null && y == soilTop - flower.second - 1 -> BLOSSOM flower != null && y >= soilTop - flower.second -> STEM else -> SKY } } // Every 3x3 window, deduped. wrapY = false: wrapping vertically would teach it that soil sits // above sky, which is the one thing this source is trying to say is untrue. val patterns = source.toBufferedImage().sliceIntoOverlappingPatterns(3, 3, wrapX = true, wrapY = false) val rules = patterns.toRules() // Named outW/outH, not w/h: inside a lambda that has its own receiver (solveWithRetries' prepare // block below), a bare `h` resolves to the Box's own frame height rather than to this local. val outW = 60 val outH = 16 // WFC has no notion of absolute position. Left alone it will happily satisfy every rule with // "soil everywhere", which is a perfectly legal tiling of this pattern set. val free = WfcSolver(outW, outH, rules, seed = 9L) free.solveWithRetries(maxAttempts = 30) val freeOut = patterns.toImg(free.resolvedTileGridOrNull()!!, outW, outH) // So pin the boundary: the classic WFC "ground" constraint. It is a correct answer (every 3×3 window in it appears in the source and every neighbouring pair agrees on its overlap), and it has no ground at all: a sky full of flowers whose stems run off the bottom edge with nothing to grow out of. Nothing in an adjacency table can say where anything belongs, so "the soil goes at the bottom" is not a fact this model has access to. Pinning the top and bottom rows with `forceTile` supplies it, and the bottom panel is what the same rules produce once they have it. The bottom panel's flowers are not the source's flowers: different columns, different heights, more of them than the source had. But every blossom sits on a stem, and the soil runs unbroken along the bottom, because those are 3×3-local facts and the model enforces them. Note that `reset()` clears the whole wave, forced cells included. Boundary conditions therefore have to be re-applied on every retry, and `solveWithRetries` takes a `prepare` block to do it in. ## Neighborhoods beyond von Neumann `WfcNeighborhood` is a set of relative offsets plus the guarantee that every offset has its opposite in the set. `VonNeumann` is four offsets; `Moore` is eight; `chebyshev(r)` and `manhattan(r)` generate the obvious families, and `WfcNeighborhood.of(WfcOffset(2, 0), WfcOffset(-2, 0))` is as legitimate as either. The neighborhood is used for *both* learning and propagation, so widening it means the model observes more relations in the source and then enforces more of them in the output. Whether that matters depends entirely on whether the source has structure along the new offsets. That is the right amount of work for a figure on a page and far too much for the thing you actually do a hundred times an hour while live coding, which is: look at the object. So `WfcSolver` implements `ToHTML`. Evaluating a solver (as a box's last expression, or via `.h` anywhere) draws its state instead of a reflective property tree. No tile set is needed, because none of these panels claims to show the tileset's colours:

The `1 × 1` tile model does what the [terrain](#learning-from-an-image-the-simple-tiled-model) did: every pair is legal, and the result is speckle. Pinning the border to the lowest level keeps it from plateauing, but a single value per cell carries no information about slope, so the interior is noise rather than the source's smooth ramp. The `3 × 3` pattern model uses its context: the result is smooth, with coherent bands. But they are horizontal bands, where the source was a concentric island. Over most of a concentric island a 3 × 3 window says "the level changes vertically and is constant horizontally", because the wide top and bottom contribute far more windows than the curved left and right edges. The model reproduced the most common local arrangement and tiled the plane with it. The readout in the box measures this as the difference between neighbouring values along rows and down columns. ### Taking the orientation out of the model The bottom row of the figure fixes this. The banding is there because the model learned *which way up the source was*, so take orientation out of the model. `expandSymmetry` closes a pattern set under the symmetry group of the square: every window plus its three rotations, each with its mirror, deduplicated, with each pattern's observed weight shared out across its orbit so the expansion does not change how likely any arrangement is. One line, applied to the pattern set rather than the solver: ```diffstatic {data-lang=kotlin} val symmetric = patterns.expandSymmetry(WfcSymmetry.All) ``` The stripes become plateaus, basins and ridges: something you would accept as a heightfield. The pattern count roughly triples here, and both the rule-learning cost (every pattern compared against every other) and the per-step entropy scan grow with it. # MorphoHDL in Field

[MorphoHDL](https://paradigms-of-intelligence.github.io/morpho/) (Apache-2) is a hardware description language
built on recursive cell division. You write a cell that halves its inputs and calls itself; the
compiler keeps dividing until a `SPLIT` runs out of bits, and the recursion bottoms out into a
fallback. Bus widths are never declared: a 32-bit adder and an 8-bit adder are the same eleven
lines of source, and the difference is entirely in how far the division ran.

**None of MorphoHDL is reimplemented.** Field runs upstream's parser, upstream's compiler and
upstream's layout kernel, byte-identical to
[commit `3ff923f`](https://github.com/paradigms-of-intelligence/morpho/tree/3ff923f9fafcb5b97ad2ef393795c96710ed00ea),
and supplies only the things a language needs from an environment rather than from itself:
simulation, drawing, and somewhere to be typed.

A `morpho` box takes upstream's source directly, and a Kotlin box can compile a design with
`morphoCircuit(...)` in a few lines; both are under [Using it](#using-it), straight after the
pictures.

---

## What it looks like

Four designs out of morpho's standard library, compiled through GraalJS, laid out by morpho's WASM
kernel in 3D, and drawn by Field as vector `FLine`s. Wire colour is **signal arrival time**: dark
where a value is known early, bright on the critical path. The gradient in each panel is that
circuit's own logic depth. Blue dots are input ports, orange are outputs.

```diffstatic_runner {data-lang=kotlin screenshot="assets/morpho_examples/family.png" wait="34.0" capture="box" open-outputs="true" padding="20"}
:::static
import afield.lang.morpho.*

// Each panel gets its OWN window: these are four different circuits at four different sizes, and a
// shared frame would shrink the shifter to a speck to fit the multiplier. Where a shared frame IS
// required -- the two adders below, the three projections further down -- it is used and said so.
val designs = [
    Triple("ripple_adder", intArrayOf(16, 16, 1), "carry chain"),
    Triple("brent_kung_adder", intArrayOf(16, 16, 1), "prefix tree"),
    Triple("right_shifter", intArrayOf(32, 5, 1), "mux cascade"),
    Triple("wallace_multiplier", intArrayOf(8, 8), "compression tree")
]

val panels = designs.map { (design, sig, kind) ->
    val c = morphoCircuit(design, *sig)
    c.growFully(relaxSteps = 220)
    println("%-20s %4d gates  depth %2d  z/xy %.2f  (%s)".format(
        design, c.netlist.gateCount, c.depth.toInt(), c.layout.flatness(), kind))
    "%s(%s) — %d gates, depth %d".format(design, sig.joinToString(","), c.netlist.gateCount, c.depth.toInt()) to
        c.flines(fit = true)
}

// fit = true normalises each panel into the unit square, which is the only way showPlaneGrid can
// frame four differently-sized circuits independently: it takes one window for the whole grid.
showPlaneGrid(*panels.toTypedArray(), columns = 2, cellWidth = 430, cellHeight = 430,
    window = morphoUnitWindow())

The shapes are the algorithms, up to a point. The ripple adder is a chain because a carry has to walk
the whole width, and the Brent–Kung is a branching tree because that is the entire point of a
parallel-prefix adder. But a force-directed layout draws *connectivity*, not a schematic: it will not
lay the shifter out as five tidy stages just because it shifts by 1, 2, 4, 8 and 16.

What the shifter shows instead is in the colour. Its 160 gates are nearly all bright, because its
depth is 5 and almost everything settles at once. The ripple adder's gates run the whole ramp from
dark to bright instead, because a 16-bit carry chain is 16 levels deep. Where the geometry stops
being informative, the arrival time takes over.

## Using it

### As a language

Set a box's main language to **MorphoHDL** and its children become morpho boxes. A morpho box is
MorphoHDL source plus one Field directive:

```diffstatic_runner {data-lang=morpho screenshot="assets/morpho_examples/as-a-language.png" wait="26.0" capture="box" open-outputs="true" padding="20"}
# main ripple_adder(8, 8, 1)

Xor3 = LUT(3, 0b1001_0110)
Maj3 = LUT(3, 0b1110_1000)

@morpho
def full_adder(a, b, c_in):
    sum = Xor3(a, b, c_in)
    c_out = Maj3(a, b, c_in)
    return sum, c_out

@morpho(fallback=full_adder)
def ripple_adder(a, b, c):
    a0, a1 = SPLIT(a)
    b0, b1 = SPLIT(b)
    s0, c_mid = ripple_adder(a0, b0, c)
    s1, c_out = ripple_adder(a1, b1, c_mid)
    sum = CAT(s0, s1)
    return sum, c_out
```

The directive is a `#` comment, which morpho's tokenizer discards, so the same file still parses in

## Whether the circuits are right

The compiled circuits are checked two ways. Field simulates them against integer arithmetic,
exhaustively for the 8-bit ripple adder, where a wiring mistake would show only on the rare input
whose carry runs the full width. And their gate counts match morpho's separate Python
implementation, `tiny_morpho.py`, gate for gate on the adders, the multiplier and the shifter.

---

## What a circuit costs to compile and simulate

The largest design here, a 4 144-gate `medusa(36,8)`, compiles and fully expands in about 270 ms
once Graal has warmed up; a 32-bit Brent–Kung adder takes about 50 ms. Relaxing the layout 200 steps
costs between about 20 ms and 1.5 s depending on size, and you rarely want it in one go —
`step(grow, relax)` in a `loop` spreads it over frames.

Simulation is bit-parallel: each net holds a `Long` whose bit *s* is that net's value for sample
*s*, so one LUT evaluation covers 64 inputs at once, and the exhaustive 8-bit adder check takes a
fraction of a second.

# MorphoHDL in Field

[MorphoHDL](https://paradigms-of-intelligence.github.io/morpho/) (Apache-2) is a hardware description language
built on recursive cell division. You write a cell that halves its inputs and calls itself; the
compiler keeps dividing until a `SPLIT` runs out of bits, and the recursion bottoms out into a
fallback. Bus widths are never declared: a 32-bit adder and an 8-bit adder are the same eleven
lines of source, and the difference is entirely in how far the division ran.

**None of MorphoHDL is reimplemented.** Field runs upstream's parser, upstream's compiler and
upstream's layout kernel, byte-identical to
[commit `3ff923f`](https://github.com/paradigms-of-intelligence/morpho/tree/3ff923f9fafcb5b97ad2ef393795c96710ed00ea),
and supplies only the things a language needs from an environment rather than from itself:
simulation, drawing, and somewhere to be typed.

A `morpho` box takes upstream's source directly, and a Kotlin box can compile a design with
`morphoCircuit(...)` in a few lines; both are under [Using it](#using-it), straight after the
pictures.

---

## What it looks like

Four designs out of morpho's standard library, compiled through GraalJS, laid out by morpho's WASM
kernel in 3D, and drawn by Field as vector `FLine`s. Wire colour is **signal arrival time**: dark
where a value is known early, bright on the critical path. The gradient in each panel is that
circuit's own logic depth. Blue dots are input ports, orange are outputs.

```diffstatic_runner {data-lang=kotlin screenshot="assets/morpho_examples/family.png" wait="34.0" capture="box" open-outputs="true" padding="20"}

    Triple("ripple_adder", intArrayOf(16, 16, 1), "carry chain"),
    Triple("brent_kung_adder", intArrayOf(16, 16, 1), "prefix tree"),

```diffstatic_runner {data-lang=morpho screenshot="assets/morpho_examples/as-a-language.png" wait="26.0" capture="box" open-outputs="true" padding="20"}

    c_out = Maj3(a, b, c_in)
    return sum, c_out

    b0, b1 = SPLIT(b)

# OSCQuery: controls other tools can find

[OSC](osc.md) sends values to an address, but the sender has to know the address, the type and
the range in advance. **OSCQuery** lets a program publish that list itself. It serves its
parameters as JSON over HTTP, announces itself on the local network, and pushes changes to
anyone listening. TouchDesigner (the *OSCQuery* COMP), Max (`oscquery` packages), Chataigne, VDMX,
ossia score and the python and JavaScript libraries all speak it.

`afield.io.osc.query` does it in both directions. A box can publish parameters that those tools
list, show as controls and set. A box can also open another program's OSCQuery service and read,
set and follow its parameters.

The [`oscquery_demo`](agent_transcripts.md#oscquery_demo) starting point runs with nothing else
running: one box publishes, and two others connect back to it as a remote.

## Publishing parameters

This box publishes a filter cutoff, an on/off switch and a scene menu, and keeps each in a
variable that other programs can set:

```diffstatic {data-lang=kotlin}

var cutoff = 1000.0
var on = true

val q = oscQuery("My piece")
q.float("/synth/cutoff", 20.0..20000.0, cutoff, "filter cutoff in Hz") { cutoff = it }
q.bool("/synth/on", on) { on = it }

```

toggle for `on` and a menu for the scene.

`oscPort`. `httpPort = 0` picks a free one; `q.httpPort` and `q.oscPort` say which. Every box asking
for the same port shares one service, so several boxes can each publish their own parameters to it.

What another program reads is plain JSON. Any HTTP client sees it, including one in a box. This
one asks for a free port, so it does not collide with a service already on 9020:

```diffstatic_runner {data-lang=kotlin screenshot="assets/oscquery/served_json.png" embed=true w="760" h="50" wait="1.5" timeout="90" name="oscquery-served-json" alt="The JSON the service returns for /synth/cutoff on one line: FULL_PATH /synth/cutoff, TYPE f, ACCESS 3, VALUE [1000.0], RANGE min 20.0 max 20000.0, DESCRIPTION filter cutoff in Hz"}

import java.net.URI
import java.net.http.*

and a half:

```diffstatic {data-lang=kotlin}

Like Field's other [OSC](osc.md) inputs, the service listens on every network interface, so

- OSC over TCP is not offered; values arrive over UDP or as binary frames on the WebSocket.
- `PATH_RENAMED` is never sent; a rename is a `PATH_REMOVED` and a `PATH_ADDED`.
- Discovery does not resolve a name clash: two services with the same name on one network both

## See also

- [OSC](osc.md), for sending and receiving plain OSC messages.
- [MQTT](mqtt.md), for sensors and devices that publish through a broker.
- [Driving lights](dmx_lighting.md), for Art-Net and sACN output.
